newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. senators find N.Korean capital a "drab" place.
newsitem.headline: U.S. senators find N.Korean capital a "drab" place.

text.p: Five U.S. senators just back from North Korea on Saturday portrayed the capital of Pyongyang as a "very drab" place where you can't get a warm room.
They also said that in their brief 24-hour visit they did not see a live chicken, pig, duck or goose, symbolising famine conditions in a nation of 22 million after two years of floods.
But the senators saw no sign of malnutrition and officials they spoke to rejected notions of a power struggle.
The visit was made as North Korea edges towards joining peace talks with South Korea, China, and the United States about formally ending the 1950-53 Korean War.

As part of the welcome for U.S. decision-makers making a rare visit to the world's last Stalinist state, the senators ran into a full-scale military mobilisation, apparently staged for their benefit. Residents told them it was the biggest in 18 months.
"I saw their city as a very drab place," Senator Pete Domenici (R-New Mexico), told a news conference in Tokyo when the five arrived from Pyongyang on a U.S. Air Force plane.
"It seemed to me they live in a very different reality than we do," he said, pointing to what he felt were exaggerated fears of an attack by U.S.-backed military forces in South Korea.

The group -- Domenici, Ted Stevens (R-Alaska), Daniel Inouye (D-Hawaii), Thad Cochran (R-Mississippi), and Pat Roberts (R-Kansas) -- are all members of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, a key player in U.S. aid efforts.
Stevens, chairman of the committee and leader of the delegation, said he was struck by how North Korea's fuel shortages have turned the capital into a frigid zone.
"We weren't in a heated building the whole time it seemed to me," said Stevens, whose Alaska State is one of the coldest places in the United States.
Domenici was amazed by the lack of cars in the capital and even more bemused by camouflage netting that covered nearly every vehicle because of the mobilisation.
"The streets of that city are spacious but there's hardly a car around," he said. "We hardly saw one vehicle that didn't have camouflage on it."
Domenici said that during the visit the city was gripped by a "total mobilization."
"We were told that they had been through an exercise in having their population go into underground tunnels and shelters," he added.
The senators said one foreign resident told them that for the first time in 18 months two waves of North Korean jet fighters also flew over the capital.
In the only visit outside Pyongyang to a nearby cooperative farm, the senators were shocked to see no livestock production.
"There was not a chicken, there was not a pig, there was not a duck, there was not a goose and it did not seem to us that there were ready foodstuffs of that nature," said Roberts.
But he added:"We didn't see evidence of malnutrition."
Roberts found "very outdated" machinery during the visit to the Chilgol Branch farm which is run by 1,400 workers.
"It's obvious that this country, to become self-reliant, will have to make great progress....," he said.
However, like the other senators, Roberts said there seemed no morale problems in the officials they met.
"They are quite forceful in saying their system is not collapsing and that the people are not mad with the leadership," he said.
